Lessons.Title: Inputs and Outputs
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: invent, test and communicate rules that assign an output to each input, including numerical and nonnumerical examples.

A rule may double an input, subtract a constant, or attach a categorical label. Specify the input set and what the rule produces; one input must not silently lead to contradictory outputs when a deterministic rule is intended.

Partner task: describe a hidden rule using three input-output pairs and ask a peer to predict two more. Multiple rules may fit only three examples, so give additional evidence rather than pretending the pattern is uniquely determined. Teacher review examines rule clarity.

Original first-party Edulytiks explanation based on publicly available Open Up Resources / Illustrative Mathematics 2017–2019, CC BY 4.0; source: https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/3/5/1/preparation.html . Publisher artwork and assessment questions are not reproduced.

KeyConcepts.Title: Input
KeyConcepts.Definition: The quantity or item supplied to a rule.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Use x as an optional symbol.

KeyConcepts.Title: Output
KeyConcepts.Definition: The result assigned by the chosen rule.

KeyConcepts.Title: Rule description
KeyConcepts.Definition: A clear operation connecting input and output.

WorkedExamples.Title: Apply a rule
WorkedExamples.Question: Rule f(x)=2x+1. Find f(4).

WorkedExamples.Title: Find missing input
WorkedExamples.Question: f(x)=3x−2 gives 13. What is x?

WorkedExamples.Title: Rule ambiguity
WorkedExamples.Question: Pairs (1,2),(2,4),(3,6) are observed. Is doubling the only possible rule?
Steps: Another expression can agree at x=1,2,3 but differ elsewhere.
More evidence or an explicit rule is needed.
WorkedExamples.Answer: No; doubling is one possible rule.
WorkedExamples.Check: For example 2x+(x−1)(x−2)(x−3) matches these pairs but differs at x=4.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Inferring a unique formula from a few pairs.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Several rules may fit finite observations.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Confusing input and output.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Reversing variables changes the mapping.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Label both sides of each pair.

SummaryPoints: A rule assigns outputs to inputs.
Use clear input and output labels.
Examples alone may not uniquely determine a rule.

Visuals.Title: Inputs and outputs of f(x)=2x+1
Visuals.Description: Original lesson-example input-output table. Each row uses y = 2x + 1. Plotting this relation, when required, is a separate graphical task.

Lessons.Title: Introduction to Functions
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: recognize a function as a relationship assigning exactly one output to each input in its domain, even though different inputs may share an output.

Use a table or mapping diagram. A repeated input with two different outputs is not a function; repeated outputs for different inputs are allowed. Ask whether a learner’s original mapping can be reconstructed unambiguously.

Design an original mapping using three named students and their birth month; each student has one assigned month, but multiple students can share a month. A teacher reviews the mapping’s domain and ambiguity.

Original first-party Edulytiks explanation based on publicly available Open Up Resources / Illustrative Mathematics 2017–2019, CC BY 4.0; source: https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/3/5/2/preparation.html . Publisher artwork and assessment questions are not reproduced.

KeyConcepts.Title: Function
KeyConcepts.Definition: Each allowed input has exactly one output.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Never assign two distinct outputs to one input.

KeyConcepts.Title: Domain
KeyConcepts.Definition: Set of inputs on which the function is defined.
KeyConcepts.Example: For f(x)=1/x the input 0 is excluded.

KeyConcepts.Title: Shared output
KeyConcepts.Definition: Different inputs can map to the same output.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Uniqueness is required per input, not per output.

WorkedExamples.Title: Recognize a function
WorkedExamples.Question: Pairs (1,2),(2,3),(1,4) form a relation. Is it a function?
Steps: One input has two outputs, violating the definition.
WorkedExamples.Check: The mapping of input 1 is not unique.

WorkedExamples.Title: Shared output allowed
WorkedExamples.Question: Pairs (1,4),(2,4),(3,9). Is it a function?
Steps: Each has exactly one assigned output.
Two inputs happen to share output 4, which is allowed.
WorkedExamples.Check: The function requirement concerns one output per input.

WorkedExamples.Title: Find domain exception
WorkedExamples.Question: Why is f(x)=1/x undefined at x=0?
Steps: Thus zero is not in the real domain.
WorkedExamples.Answer: 0 is excluded from the real domain.
WorkedExamples.Check: Every other real x gives one output.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Requiring all outputs to be different.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Multiple inputs may share an output.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Ignoring inputs where an equation is undefined.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A function must have a legitimate output for every input in its stated domain.

SummaryPoints: A function assigns one output to each input.
Repeated outputs are permitted.
State the domain.

Lessons.Title: Equations for Functions
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: evaluate a function from an equation for specified inputs and, when possible, solve an equation to find input(s) that produce a given output.
Use notation f(3) for the output when input is 3, not multiplication by f. A linear function is one-to-one when slope is nonzero, but f(x)=x² can produce one output from two inputs.
Compare f(x)=2x−5 and g(x)=x² with positive and negative inputs. Teacher review checks clear notation and explanation of why inverse output questions may have multiple answers.

Original first-party Edulytiks explanation based on publicly available Open Up Resources / Illustrative Mathematics 2017–2019, CC BY 4.0; source: https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/3/5/3/preparation.html . Publisher artwork and assessment questions are not reproduced.

KeyConcepts.Title: Function notation
KeyConcepts.Definition: f(a) denotes the output at x=a.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Substitute a into every x in the rule.

KeyConcepts.Title: Solve for input
KeyConcepts.Definition: Find x from a specified output y.

KeyConcepts.Title: Multiple preimages
KeyConcepts.Definition: Distinct inputs may have the same output.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Reverse questions may have several answers.

WorkedExamples.Title: Evaluate affine function
WorkedExamples.Question: For f(x)=2x−5, find f(3).

WorkedExamples.Title: Solve for input
WorkedExamples.Question: f(x)=2x−5. Which x gives output 9?

WorkedExamples.Title: Two inputs same output
WorkedExamples.Question: For g(x)=x², find all real x with g(x)=9.
Steps: Real solutions are x=−3 and x=3.
WorkedExamples.Check: Squaring erases sign.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treating f(3) as f times 3.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Function notation means evaluation.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Reporting only positive square root.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A square may have positive and negative preimages.

SummaryPoints: Evaluate by substitution.
Inverse input questions may be nonunique.
Notation identifies input and output precisely.

Visuals.Title: Evaluation of a linear function
Visuals.Description: Original lesson-example input-output table. Each row uses y = 2x − 5. Plotting this relation, when required, is a separate graphical task.

Lessons.Title: Tables, Equations, and Graphs of Functions
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: connect a function equation with numerical table pairs and their plotted points in the coordinate plane.

For y=x², table outputs at −2,−1,0,1,2 are 4,1,0,1,4. The graph is curved rather than a line; a function need not be linear. A vertical line intersects the graph at most once for each x in its domain.
Plot the square rule with labeled axes, join points smoothly based on the real domain, and distinguish the exact equation from sparse observations. Teacher review checks axes and the curve.

Original first-party Edulytiks explanation based on publicly available Open Up Resources / Illustrative Mathematics 2017–2019, CC BY 4.0; source: https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/3/5/4/preparation.html . Publisher artwork and assessment questions are not reproduced.

KeyConcepts.Title: Table row
KeyConcepts.Definition: A point (x,f(x)) from a function.

KeyConcepts.Title: Graph
KeyConcepts.Definition: Visual representation of all allowed input-output pairs.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Plot x horizontally and f(x) vertically.

KeyConcepts.Title: Vertical-line property
KeyConcepts.Definition: A function has no two outputs at the same x.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Any vertical line intersects a function graph at most once.
KeyConcepts.Example: A circle fails this test over most x values.

WorkedExamples.Title: Complete square table
WorkedExamples.Question: Find x² for x=−2,−1,0,1,2.
WorkedExamples.Check: Positive and negative equal magnitudes share outputs.

WorkedExamples.Title: Check plotted point
WorkedExamples.Question: Is (−3,9) on y=x²?
WorkedExamples.Check: Negative x is permitted.

WorkedExamples.Title: Reject point
WorkedExamples.Question: Is (2,5) on y=x²?
Steps: The point is not on the graph.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Joining x² table points into a straight line.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The rate is not constant.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use a smooth curve matching the rule.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Swapping x and y when plotting.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: It changes the graph.

SummaryPoints: Equation, table and graph encode the same function.
Functions need not be linear.
Use exact substitution to check plotted points.

Visuals.Title: Quadratic values are not linear
Visuals.Description: Opposite inputs share the same square. Plotting the curve remains a separate graphic task.

Lessons.Title: More Graphs of Functions
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: interpret values, change and meaningful coordinates from an existing function graph rather than assuming every graph is linear.

A graph with time on its horizontal axis and distance on its vertical axis can rise, remain flat or fall. Interpret the coordinates and rates in context; a line segment rising twice as fast has twice the slope when the scales are identical.
Compare a journey: start at 0 km, reach 6 km at 2 hours, stay until 3 hours, then return to 0 km by 5 hours. Teacher reviews the graph and story correspondence.

Original first-party Edulytiks explanation based on publicly available Open Up Resources / Illustrative Mathematics 2017–2019, CC BY 4.0; source: https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/3/5/5/preparation.html . Publisher artwork and assessment questions are not reproduced.

KeyConcepts.Title: Graph reading
KeyConcepts.Definition: A point (t,d) gives output d at input t.
KeyConcepts.Example: At (2,6), distance is 6 km after 2 h.

KeyConcepts.Title: Flat interval
KeyConcepts.Definition: Constant output over a range.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Slope zero shows no change in measured quantity.
KeyConcepts.Example: Distance stays 6 km from t=2 to t=3.

KeyConcepts.Title: Decreasing interval
KeyConcepts.Definition: Output falls as input increases.

WorkedExamples.Title: Rate outward
WorkedExamples.Question: Distance rises from 0 to 6 km in 2 hours. Average rate?
WorkedExamples.Check: A constant straight segment has that slope.

WorkedExamples.Title: Stop duration
WorkedExamples.Question: Distance stays 6 km between t=2 and t=3. How long is the stop?
WorkedExamples.Check: Graph is horizontal during the stop.

WorkedExamples.Title: Return rate
WorkedExamples.Question: Distance decreases from 6 to 0 in 2 hours. Slope?
WorkedExamples.Check: Negative slope means returning toward the start, not physically negative speed.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Confusing decreasing distance from start with negative travel speed.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Slope sign describes distance-from-start change, not necessarily speed sign.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Ignoring a flat interval.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Flat distance means unchanged position with respect to start in this model.

SummaryPoints: Read axes and coordinates in context.
Horizontal segments show constant output.
Signed slope describes direction of output change.

Lessons.Title: Even More Graphs of Functions
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: sketch a function graph from a verbal story while identifying where output increases, decreases or remains constant.

A story specifies key time events, initial and final values, and possible rates. Put these anchor points on axes before joining them. A sketch may only be qualitative if no exact numerical rates are given.
Draw an original tank-fill story: 0 L at minute 0, 12 L at minute 3, a pause to minute 5, then 20 L at minute 7. Explain the graph segments and why a teacher must evaluate the written interpretation.

Original first-party Edulytiks explanation based on publicly available Open Up Resources / Illustrative Mathematics 2017–2019, CC BY 4.0; source: https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/3/5/6/preparation.html . Publisher artwork and assessment questions are not reproduced.

KeyConcepts.Title: Anchor point
KeyConcepts.Definition: A known time-output pair in a story.

KeyConcepts.Title: Piecewise rate
KeyConcepts.Definition: Slope can change between time intervals.

KeyConcepts.Title: Pause
KeyConcepts.Definition: An interval with constant output.
KeyConcepts.Example: Volume remains 12 L from minute 3 to 5.

WorkedExamples.Title: First fill rate
WorkedExamples.Question: Tank from 0 to 12 L over minutes 0 to 3. What rate?
WorkedExamples.Check: The first segment joins (0,0) and (3,12).

WorkedExamples.Title: Pause rate
WorkedExamples.Question: Volume stays 12 L from t=3 to t=5. What rate?
WorkedExamples.Check: This segment is horizontal.

WorkedExamples.Title: Final fill
WorkedExamples.Question: Volume increases 12 to 20 L between t=5 and 7. Rate?
WorkedExamples.Check: The last segment has the same slope as the first.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Joining all event points with one straight line.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: It erases the pause.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Not labeling time and volume units.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: An unlabeled graph is ambiguous.

SummaryPoints: Use story events as graph anchors.
Describe each rate separately.
Some sketches need teacher-reviewed qualitative reasoning.

Lessons.Title: Connecting Representations of Functions
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: connect a function’s story, table, graph and algebraic rule, with consistent inputs, outputs and units across all representations.
Given a constant fee of $5 plus $2 per ticket, construct f(n)=5+2n. A table for n=0,1,2,3 produces $5,$7,$9,$11, and a graph shows these discrete points for whole-number ticket counts.
Compare the plotted points with a continuous line and explain why fractional tickets are not physically meaningful. Teacher review checks the correspondence and restrictions.

Original first-party Edulytiks explanation based on publicly available Open Up Resources / Illustrative Mathematics 2017–2019, CC BY 4.0; source: https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/3/5/7/preparation.html . Publisher artwork and assessment questions are not reproduced.

KeyConcepts.Title: Story-to-rule
KeyConcepts.Definition: Translate fixed and per-unit contributions.

KeyConcepts.Title: Rule-to-table
KeyConcepts.Definition: Evaluate permitted inputs.

KeyConcepts.Title: Discrete domain
KeyConcepts.Definition: Inputs count indivisible items.
KeyConcepts.Example: Ticket counts 0,1,2,… rather than arbitrary decimals.

WorkedExamples.Title: Build a table
WorkedExamples.Question: For f(n)=5+2n, find outputs for n=0,1,2,3.
WorkedExamples.Check: Successive outputs rise by $2.

WorkedExamples.Title: Find counted tickets
WorkedExamples.Question: Total $15 under f(n)=5+2n. How many?

WorkedExamples.Title: Reject fraction-ticket point
WorkedExamples.Question: Does n=2.5 represent a feasible ticket count?
Steps: Tickets are indivisible in this model.
2.5 is outside the intended input domain.
WorkedExamples.Answer: No, not a valid ticket count.
WorkedExamples.Check: Discrete input domain is nonnegative integers.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Drawing a continuous solid line as though half-tickets are real.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The story has discrete inputs.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Forgetting fixed cost at zero input.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Intercept is nonzero.

SummaryPoints: Keep all representations consistent.
Interpret intercept and per-unit change.
Match the input domain to the story.

Visuals.Title: A fixed term plus rate
Visuals.Description: Original lesson-example input-output table. Each row uses y = 2x + 5. Plotting this relation, when required, is a separate graphical task.

Lessons.Title: Linear Functions
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: identify linear functions from constant rates of change and distinguish them from functions whose differences vary.
For equally spaced x-values, a linear function produces equal differences in f(x); a quadratic function generally does not. Interpret slope and intercept from a table, graph or equation.
Compare two input-output tables: f(x)=3x+2 and g(x)=x². Write evidence based on differences. Teacher reviews the explanation and the selected representative points.

Original first-party Edulytiks explanation based on publicly available Open Up Resources / Illustrative Mathematics 2017–2019, CC BY 4.0; source: https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/3/5/8/preparation.html . Publisher artwork and assessment questions are not reproduced.

KeyConcepts.Title: Constant first difference
KeyConcepts.Definition: Equal input steps yield equal output changes.
KeyConcepts.Example: f(x)=3x+2 increases by 3 per x unit.

KeyConcepts.Title: Linear equation
KeyConcepts.Definition: Function represented by y=mx+b.

KeyConcepts.Title: Nonlinear counterexample
KeyConcepts.Definition: First differences vary for equal input increments.

WorkedExamples.Title: Linear table
WorkedExamples.Question: For f(x)=3x+2, list f(0),f(1),f(2),f(3).
WorkedExamples.Check: Every 1-unit input increase adds 3.

WorkedExamples.Title: Quadratic table
WorkedExamples.Question: List g(x)=x² for x=0,1,2,3.
WorkedExamples.Check: First differences vary.

WorkedExamples.Title: Find intercept
WorkedExamples.Question: A linear function has slope 3 and f(2)=8. Find b.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Calling a curved function linear because it rises.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Increasing alone does not imply constant rate.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Computing differences across unequal input steps without normalizing.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Slope is change per input unit.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Divide output difference by input difference.

SummaryPoints: Constant rate gives linear behavior.
Slope and intercept describe line functions.
First differences detect nonlinear tables.

Visuals.Title: A linear function with constant rate
Visuals.Description: Original lesson-example input-output table. Each row uses y = 3x + 2. Plotting this relation, when required, is a separate graphical task.

Lessons.Title: Linear Models
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: construct a useful linear model for a real-world situation and distinguish its prediction from a guaranteed observed value.

Real data often vary. A line may approximate measurements even if the points do not lie exactly on it. State input/output units, select a sensible rate and starting value, and discuss where the model might fail.
Use independent temperature readings (0 min,20°C), (10 min,24°C), (20 min,28°C) to build T(t)=20+0.4t. Ask whether the model stays valid for many hours. A teacher judges model limitations.

Original first-party Edulytiks explanation based on publicly available Open Up Resources / Illustrative Mathematics 2017–2019, CC BY 4.0; source: https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/3/5/9/preparation.html . Publisher artwork and assessment questions are not reproduced.

KeyConcepts.Title: Linear model
KeyConcepts.Definition: A constant-rate approximation or rule for related quantities.
KeyConcepts.Rule: y≈mx+b for observed data, exact only under the stated assumption.

KeyConcepts.Title: Rate with units
KeyConcepts.Definition: Change in output per unit input.

KeyConcepts.Title: Extrapolation
KeyConcepts.Definition: Prediction outside observed input range.
KeyConcepts.Example: Predicting temperature at 3 hours from 20 minutes of data is uncertain.

WorkedExamples.Title: Compute warming rate
WorkedExamples.Question: Temperature rises from 20°C to 24°C in 10 min. Find rate.
WorkedExamples.Check: At 20 min the model predicts 28°C.

WorkedExamples.Title: Predict within range
WorkedExamples.Question: T=20+0.4t. Find T(15).
WorkedExamples.Check: Between known readings 24 and 28.

WorkedExamples.Title: Evaluate far prediction
WorkedExamples.Question: Model at t=180 minutes gives what result, and is it certain?
Steps: The reading is far outside the 0–20 min evidence range and may not be realistic.
WorkedExamples.Answer: 92°C as a mathematical extrapolation, not a verified temperature.
WorkedExamples.Check: Model assumptions need independent support.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treating a fitted line as an exact law for all times.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A model can fail outside its data range.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Forgetting units in slope.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Rate is a ratio of measured quantities.

SummaryPoints: Linear models predict with assumptions.
Rate and intercept carry units.
Extrapolation needs caution.

Lessons.Title: Piecewise Linear Functions
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: interpret and construct a function built from linear segments with different rates, verifying which rule applies on each input interval.
A piecewise function may switch from increasing to constant or decreasing at a boundary. Clear interval endpoints prevent contradictory outputs at the same input.

Model a parking fee: $3 for up to one hour, then $3 plus $2 per additional whole hour. Compare with a continuous piecewise rule if fractional hours are permitted. Teacher review checks the selected billing policy and graph step/segment choice.

Original first-party Edulytiks explanation based on publicly available Open Up Resources / Illustrative Mathematics 2017–2019, CC BY 4.0; source: https://im.kendallhunt.com/MS/teachers/3/5/10/preparation.html . Publisher artwork and assessment questions are not reproduced.

KeyConcepts.Title: Piecewise rule
KeyConcepts.Definition: Different formulas on specified input ranges.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Every allowed input must have one output.

KeyConcepts.Title: Boundary ownership
KeyConcepts.Definition: Which branch applies at a break point.
KeyConcepts.Example: At t=2 the first rule gives 4.

KeyConcepts.Title: Segment slope
KeyConcepts.Definition: Rate can differ by interval.

WorkedExamples.Title: Evaluate first branch
WorkedExamples.Question: f(t)=2t for 0≤t≤2; f(t)=4 for 2<t≤4. Find f(1).
WorkedExamples.Check: The other branch does not apply at t=1.

WorkedExamples.Title: Evaluate boundary
WorkedExamples.Question: Find f(2).
Steps: t=2 is included in first branch.
The second branch excludes t=2 but would agree at boundary.
WorkedExamples.Check: Single-valued definition is maintained.

WorkedExamples.Title: Evaluate later interval
WorkedExamples.Question: Find f(3.5).
WorkedExamples.Check: Graph is flat from after t=2 to t=4.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Applying one formula outside its interval.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The piecewise definition assigns different rules to different domains.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Assigning two contradictory boundary outputs.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A function cannot produce two values for one input.

SummaryPoints: Piecewise functions can change slope.
Check endpoint ownership.
Interpret each segment within its interval.

Visuals.Title: Two parts of one function
Visuals.Description: Rule 2t applies for 0≤t≤2; rule 4 applies for 2<t≤4. No jump occurs at t=2.
